questions.q: Calculate the overall order of a reaction which has the rate expression $\text{Rate} = k[A]^{1/2}[B]^{3/2}$.
questions.solution:
The **overall order** of a reaction is the sum of the powers to which the concentration terms are raised in the experimentally determined rate law.

Here the powers are $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $A$ and $\dfrac{3}{2}$ for $B$, so

$$\text{order} = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{3}{2} = \frac{4}{2} = \mathbf{2}.$$

The reaction is **second order overall**, though it is of order $\frac12$ with respect to $A$ and order $\frac32$ with respect to $B$.

Note that order can be fractional, zero or even negative — it is found by experiment and need not match the stoichiometric coefficients, unlike molecularity, which is always a whole number.

questions.q: A first order reaction takes $77 \cdot 78$ minutes for 50% completion. Calculate the time required for 30% completion of this reaction, in minutes, to the nearest minute. (Given $\log 10 = 1$, $\log 7 = 0 \cdot 8450$.)
questions.solution:
**Step 1 — find the rate constant from the half-life.** For a first order reaction,

$$t_{1/2} = \frac{0 \cdot 693}{k} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k = \frac{0 \cdot 693}{77 \cdot 78} = 8 \cdot 91 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{min}^{-1}.$$

**Step 2 — apply the first order integrated rate law.**

$$t = \frac{2 \cdot 303}{k}\log\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}.$$

At 30% completion, 70% of the reactant is left, so taking $[A]_0 = 100$ and $[A] = 70$ :

$$t = \frac{2 \cdot 303}{8 \cdot 91 \times 10^{-3}}\log\frac{100}{70}.$$

**Step 3 — evaluate the logarithm** using the values given :

$$\log\frac{100}{70} = \log 100 - \log 70 = 2 - (1 + 0 \cdot 8450) = 0 \cdot 1550.$$

**Step 4 — substitute.**

$$t = 258 \cdot 5 \times 0 \cdot 1550 \approx \mathbf{40}\ \text{minutes}.$$

Sensible: 30% completion is well short of the half-life, so the time must be well under $77 \cdot 78$ minutes.

questions.q: A first order reaction has a rate constant of $10^{-3}$ per second. How long will $5$ g of this reactant take to reduce to $3$ g? Give your answer in seconds, to the nearest second. (Given $\log 3 = 0 \cdot 4771$, $\log 5 = 0 \cdot 6990$.)
questions.solution:
For a first order reaction the integrated rate law is

$$t = \frac{2 \cdot 303}{k}\log\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}.$$

Because the law involves only a **ratio** of amounts, masses may be used directly — there is no need to convert to concentrations.

**Substitute** $[A]_0 = 5$ g, $[A] = 3$ g and $k = 10^{-3}\ \text{s}^{-1}$ :

$$t = \frac{2 \cdot 303}{10^{-3}}\log\frac{5}{3}.$$

**Evaluate the logarithm** from the values given :

$$\log\frac{5}{3} = \log 5 - \log 3 = 0 \cdot 6990 - 0 \cdot 4771 = 0 \cdot 2219.$$

**Finish.**

$$t = 2303 \times 0 \cdot 2219 \approx \mathbf{511}\ \text{seconds}.$$

(As a check, the half-life here is $0 \cdot 693/10^{-3} = 693$ s, and going from 5 g to 3 g is less than halving — so a time under 693 s is right.)

questions.q: For a first order reaction, the half-life:
questions.solution:
$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$ — no concentration term at all.

Start with a kilogram or a milligram and half of it is gone in the same time. This is what makes radioactive decay (first order) so useful for dating.
options: is independent of the initial concentration

questions.q: The units of the rate constant for a first order reaction are:
questions.solution:
For order $n$, the units of $k$ are $\left(\text{mol L}^{-1}\right)^{1-n}\text{s}^{-1}$.

For $n = 1$ this is simply $\mathbf{\text{s}^{-1}}$ — which is a quick way to identify the order from a given rate constant.

questions.q: According to the Arrhenius equation, the rate constant increases with temperature because:
questions.solution:
$k = Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}$.

Heating does not lower $E_{a}$; it shifts the **Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution** so that a far larger fraction of molecules carries enough energy to get over the barrier.

That exponential is why a $10$ K rise roughly doubles many reaction rates, while the collision frequency itself rises only a few per cent.
options: a larger fraction of molecules has energy above the activation energy
the order of the reaction changes

questions.q: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction by:
questions.solution:
A catalyst offers a **different route with a lower $E_{a}$**, so more molecules can make the journey.

It does **not** move the equilibrium position: it lowers the barrier for both the forward and the reverse reaction equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but at the same place. $\Delta G$ is untouched.
options: increasing the energy of the reactants
providing an alternative path of lower activation energy
shifting the equilibrium to the right

questions.q: For a reaction, rate $= k[A]^{2}[B]$. If $[A]$ is doubled and $[B]$ is halved, by what factor does the rate change?
questions.solution:
Rate $\propto [A]^{2}[B]$.

$[A]$ doubled contributes $2^{2} = 4$; $[B]$ halved contributes $\tfrac12$.

$4 \times \tfrac12 = \mathbf{2}$ — the rate doubles.

questions.q: A zero order reaction has $k = 0.02$ mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$ and an initial concentration of $0.5$ mol/L. Find the time (in s) for the reaction to go to completion.
questions.solution:
For zero order, the concentration falls linearly: $[A] = [A]_{0} - kt$.

Completion means $[A] = 0$, so $t = \dfrac{[A]_{0}}{k} = \dfrac{0.5}{0.02} = \mathbf{25}$ s.

A zero order reaction is the only kind that truly finishes — a first order one only approaches zero.

questions.q: The rate constant of a reaction has units L mol$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$. What is the order of the reaction?
questions.solution:
The general form is $\left(\text{mol L}^{-1}\right)^{1-n}\text{s}^{-1}$.

Matching $\text{L mol}^{-1}$ means $1 - n = -1$, so $n = \mathbf{2}$ — second order.

questions.q: Derive the integrated rate equation for a first order reaction and show that its half-life is independent of the initial concentration.
questions.solution:
**Rate law.** $-\dfrac{d[A]}{dt} = k[A]$.

**Separate and integrate** from $[A]_{0}$ at $t = 0$ to $[A]$ at time $t$:

$\displaystyle\int_{[A]_{0}}^{[A]}\dfrac{d[A]}{[A]} = -k\int_{0}^{t}dt$

$\log_{e}\dfrac{[A]}{[A]_{0}} = -kt$, or

$\mathbf{k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[A]_{0}}{[A]}}$.

**Half-life.** Put $[A] = \dfrac{[A]_{0}}{2}$:

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{t_{1/2}}\log 2 = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}} \Rightarrow t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$.

$[A]_{0}$ has cancelled out entirely, so the half-life does not depend on how much you started with. ∎

A plot of $\log[A]$ against $t$ is a straight line of slope $-\dfrac{k}{2.303}$ — which is how first order kinetics is confirmed in practice.

questions.q: Distinguish between order and molecularity of a reaction, with an example of a reaction whose order is not equal to its molecularity.
questions.solution:
**Order** — experimental, the sum of the powers in the rate law. May be zero, fractional or negative. Applies to an overall reaction.

**Molecularity** — theoretical, the number of species colliding in **one elementary step**. Always a positive whole number, and never more than 3 in practice (a four-body collision is vanishingly unlikely).

**Example — acid hydrolysis of an ester:**

$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COOC}_{2}\text{H}_{5} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O} \to \text{CH}_{3}\text{COOH} + \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$

Two molecules react, so the molecularity is 2, but water is present in such vast excess that its concentration never measurably changes. The rate depends only on the ester:

rate $= k'[\text{ester}]$ — **order 1**, a *pseudo first order* reaction.

For a multi-step reaction, molecularity has no meaning at all for the overall change; only the individual steps have one. The order comes from the **slowest** step.

questions.q: State the Arrhenius equation, explain each term, and show how $E_{a}$ can be found graphically. The rate constant doubles when the temperature rises from $300$ K to $310$ K — estimate $E_{a}$. (Take $R = 8.314$ J K$^{-1}$mol$^{-1}$, $\log 2 = 0.301$.)
questions.solution:
**The equation.** $k = Ae^{-E_{a}/RT}$, where $A$ is the frequency factor (collisions with the right orientation) and $e^{-E_{a}/RT}$ is the fraction of collisions energetic enough to react.

**Graphical form.** Taking logarithms:

$\log k = \log A - \dfrac{E_{a}}{2.303RT}$.

A plot of $\log k$ against $\dfrac{1}{T}$ is a **straight line** of slope $-\dfrac{E_{a}}{2.303R}$ and intercept $\log A$.

**Two-temperature form:**

$\log\dfrac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} = \dfrac{E_{a}}{2.303R}\left[\dfrac{T_{2} - T_{1}}{T_{1}T_{2}}\right]$.

**Substituting** $\dfrac{k_{2}}{k_{1}} = 2$, $T_{1} = 300$, $T_{2} = 310$:

$0.301 = \dfrac{E_{a}}{2.303 \times 8.314} \times \dfrac{10}{93000}$

$E_{a} = \dfrac{0.301 \times 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 93000}{10} \approx \mathbf{53.6}$ kJ/mol.

That is a very ordinary activation energy — and it is the reason the rough rule 'rate doubles for every $10$ K' holds so often around room temperature.

questions.q: State the main postulates of collision theory and explain why not every collision leads to reaction.
questions.solution:
**Postulates.**

1. Molecules must **collide** for a reaction to occur.

2. Only collisions with energy at least $E_{a}$ — **effective collisions** — can react.

3. The colliding molecules must also be **correctly oriented** for the bonds to form and break.

Hence rate $= P \times Z \times e^{-E_{a}/RT}$, where $Z$ is the collision frequency and $P$ the steric factor.

**Why most collisions fail.** At ordinary temperatures only a tiny fraction of molecules carry energy above $E_{a}$, and of those, many meet the wrong way round.

The numbers make the point: a gas undergoes about $10^{30}$ collisions per litre per second. If every one reacted, every reaction would be over instantly. Most reactions take minutes — so the overwhelming majority of collisions achieve nothing at all.

Two cars meeting is not enough for the passengers to shake hands: they must meet hard enough to stop, and be facing the right way.

questions.q: For the reaction $2\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{5} \to 4\text{NO}_{2} + \text{O}_{2}$, write the rate of reaction in terms of each species.
questions.solution:
Divide each rate of change by the species' stoichiometric coefficient, with a minus sign for reactants:

$\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{5}]}{dt} = +\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{d[\text{NO}_{2}]}{dt} = +\dfrac{d[\text{O}_{2}]}{dt}$.

**Why the coefficients are needed:** $\text{NO}_{2}$ appears four times as fast as $\text{O}_{2}$, so without dividing, the same reaction would have four different 'rates'.

So if oxygen forms at $0.01$ mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$, then $\text{NO}_{2}$ forms at $0.04$ and $\text{N}_{2}\text{O}_{5}$ disappears at $0.02$ mol L$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$.
